Designing a user-centeredbattery disposal service

Transforming battery disposal into a seamless, rewardedfamily ritual that can increase collection rates to 60%.

 Service Design · Research Driven · System Thinking

Fermio

Batteries are small.Their impact is not.

0nly 5 out of 100batteries are properly disposed

Sustainable Development Goals are not just targetsthey are promises to our cities and health.But in 2026, we are still lagging.Fermio aims to close the gap

SDG Goal 11.6

By 2030, reduce the adverse per capita environmental impact ofcities, including by paying special attention to air quality andmunicipal and other waste management

SDG Goal 12.4

By 2020, achieve the environmentally sound management ofchemicals and all wastes throughout their life cycle, in accordancewith agreed international frameworks, and significantly reduce theirrelease to air, water and soil in order to minimize their adverseimpacts on human health and the environment

OVERVIEW

Fermio is a systemic intervention. We’ve built the bridge betweenthe people who make batteries, the government that needs totrack them, and the logistics that move them. It’s a unified loopthat makes recycling as invisible and automatic as breathing.

ROLE

Systems Thinking, Deep Research, Strategy & Prototyping

TIMELINE

10-Weeks

CHALLENGE

Recycling today is a chore. Individuals want to help, butthey’re stuck because of unawareness and distrust inexisting systems without incentives.

GOAL

How might we make e-waste recycling feel as simple andtrustworthy, encouraging families to recycle even theirsmallest electronics?

OUTCOME

By partnering with Blinkit for effortless pickup-on-deliveryand creating a digital loop for 100% traceability, we’vecleared a path to take collection rates from 5% to 60%,reducing toxic waste in our cities by 25%.

Understanding the problem

The e-waste ecosystem in India is rather unorganised

•Households prefer kabbadiwalas forinstant cash and convenience.•E-waste, especially batteries, often sitsunused for years at home.• Most electronics are designed with shortlifespans and poor repairability.• EPR laws exist, but enforcement is weak.• Companies shape disposal behavior viatrade-ins, warranties, and repair policies.• Only ~22% of e-waste is formallycollected.• E-waste contains 60+ valuable metals likegold, silver, and copper.•China and Mexico use centralised digitalsystems for e-waste tracking.

The Responsible but Distracted Recycler

Meet Arjun

27 years oldSoftware EngineerUrban / BangaloreLives with spouse and one 3-year-old childDecision Making: Usually makes disposal decisions withfamily, but action is often delayed or forgotten.

Bio

Arjun is a 27-year-old software engineer and young father juggling work and family life. He’s aware of e-waste issues but rarely finds time to act on them. A drawer at home holds old phones, tangled cables, and batteries all “to deal with later.” He trusts organized recyclers more than local dealers but hasn’t found one that feels convenient or reliable.
 💬 “I keep telling myself I’ll recycle all this stuff one weekend - but that weekend never comes.”

Slightly forgetful

Habit-prone

How Might We

make e-waste recycling feel as simple and trustworthy as orderingfrom Swiggy , encouraging families like Arjun’s to recycle even theirsmallest electronics?

User Journey Map

Did not think it would become so long

Sees or buys a device that includes abattery (phone, remote, toy, etc.).

Occasionally buys loose orreplacement batteries.

Reads product details - price,performance, or brand, not disposalinfo.

Unpacks and installs the battery.

Discards the packaging (with recycling/safety info) immediately.

STEPS

Starts using the product withoutnoting any disposal instructions.

Regularly uses the device with thebattery installed.

Recharges or replaces whenperformance drops.

Notices the battery running out fasterover time.

May try quick fixes (cleaningcontacts, recharging more often,etc.).

Eventually realizes the battery isweak or dead.

Removes the used battery and putsit aside - often without a clear plan.

Identifies that the battery no longerworks properly.

Sets the old battery aside “for later”rather than discarding it.

Begins to wonder how or where todispose of it.

Considers throwing it in the dustbin(common habit).

Remembers hearing that batteriesshouldn’t go in regular waste.

Searches online or asks others aboutdisposal options.

Realizes there are limited or unclearoptions nearby.

Often ends up keeping a smallcollection of dead batteries at home.

Decides to clear out old batteries ordevices.

Looks for available disposal routes:

Evaluates convenience - distance,timing, effort required.

If easy: drops them off at a nearbybin or gives to kabadiwala.

If not easy: delays again or mixes withregular waste.

In some cases, waits for an e-wastecollection drive or pickup event.

If giving to kabadiwala, may notknow if recycled improperly.

Once handed off, assumesresponsibility ends there.

(Formal route) Authorized recycler -processes for material recovery.

(Informal route) Battery dismantledor sold; potential pollution.

User typically has no visibility intowhat happens next.

Occasionally sees campaigns,or gov.messaging about recycling.

Gains surface-level awareness that properrecycling prevents harm

Arjun browses an electronics store or e-commerce app, exploring gadgets thatcome with removable batteries.

Arjun grabs a pack of AA/AAAbatteries from a nearby conveniencestore during errands.

Arjun compares brands online,reading specifications like voltage,shelf life, and cost.

Arjun opens the packaging, insertsthe battery into the device, andstarts using it immediately.

Arjun throws away the wrapper or blisterpack after unpacking, not noticingprinted information.

Storyboard / Visual

Arjun begins using the newdevice normally, unaware of anyrecycling or return process.

Arjun uses daily devices - TVremote, headphones, or clock -powered by batteries.

Arjun notices low power and eitherrecharges a device or replacesdisposable batteries.

Arjun observes that recharges don’t lastas long, or devices need replacementbatteries more often.

Arjun attempts small DIY fixes -wipes terminals, swaps batteryorder, recharges repeatedly.

Device fails completely; Arjunconcludes the battery has reachedthe end of its life.

Arjun removes the old battery andplaces it in a drawer, telling himselfhe’ll deal with it later.

Arjun tries to use a device but it failsrepeatedly - confirms that thebattery is dead.

Arjun tosses the used battery into adrawer or corner, thinking he’llhandle it another day.

Arjun recalls hearing that batteriesshouldn’t go into regular bins; startsthinking about safe disposal.

Arjun stands near the bin, hesitatingbetween convenience andenvironmental responsibility.

A memory resurfaces - a past ad,school lesson, or social post abouthazardous waste.

Arjun types “where to recyclebatteries near me” or asks in acommunity group.

Arjun checks maps or localities andfinds no visible or verified collectioncenters.

Drawer or box at home with severalold batteries stored indefinitely.

Arjun opens his drawer and decidesit’s time to declutter old devices andused batteries.

Arjun weighs multiple disposaloptions - which one is easiest andmost trustworthy.

Arjun checks how far the nearestcenter is or when the next drive isscheduled.

Arjun visits a local scrap dealer ordeposit point and hands over thebatteries.

Arjun, unable to find a nearby bin orconvenient option, tosses the batteryinto general waste.

Arjun saves the batteries in a bag,waiting for a school, office, ormunicipal collection event.

Arjun hands over items to a localscrap dealer, assuming they’ll handlethem correctly.

Arjun walks away after disposal,feeling he’s done his part.

The collected battery reaches anauthorized recycling facility; extractmetals like lithium, cobalt, and nickel.

Informal recyclers manuallydismantle batteries for recoverablemetals

Arjun assumes the battery isresponsibly handled but neverchecks or receives confirmation.

Arjun sees a posts about e-wasteawareness or recycling successstories on social media

Arjun knows recycling is beneficial butreverts to convenience-first disposal habits.

Description of theExperience

Battery disposal awarenessremains nonexistent - no cuesor reminders embedded in userexperience.

The battery is invisible in the userexperience

The user sees battery degradationas a maintenance task, not anenvironmental issue.

Signs of end-of-life appear, but Arjundoesn’t yet consider disposal orrecycling options.

Tries to extend product life, but lacksknowledge about battery lifespan orsafe disposal practices.

Sees disposal as an afterthought -the focus is replacement, notresponsible handling.

Common behavior of postponement;used batteries start accumulatingwith no clear disposal strategy.

User awareness shifts fromfunctionality to EOL recognition, butdisposal knowledge is still absent.

A common “holding pattern”behavior - user postpones disposaldue to lack of accessible solutions

Awareness transition stage - userbegins information-seeking butlacks clear guidance channels.

The user’s environmental valuesclash with habits; lack ofconvenience leads to rationalizingimproper disposal.

External knowledge triggersreflection, but without accessiblenext steps, motivation fades.

User attempts to act but findsunclear or outdated guidance,decreasing confidence to proceed.

Environmental intent collapses dueto lack of accessible infrastructure -a key barrier in the user journey.

Becomes an unintentional“temporary landfill.” Habit normalizesthe inaction.

The decision marks a key behavioralshift - from awareness to intent.

Awareness meets friction - unclearwhich option is correct oraccessible.

Decision depends largely on ease;low-effort systems correlate withhigher compliance.

User feels responsible and fulfilled;however, lacks understanding ofwhat happens next in the chain.

The critical behavioral breakdown point;lack of convenience overridesenvironmental intent.

Relies on external triggers (events orreminders) rather than continuoushabit.

Informal recycling network absorbsthe item, but low user visibility andconfidence in proper recycling

The mental model ends at handoff -disconnect between personal actionand environmental outcome.

The system works efficiently - butmost users (like Arjun) have novisibility into it.

High environmental risk - lack oftraceability allows improperrecycling and leakage of pollutants.

The information gap weakens theemotional reward of responsiblebehavior, reducing habit formation.

messages reinforce moralcorrectness but fail to sustainbehavioral change.

structural barriers and lack of incentivesoutweigh environmental intent.

OVERVIEW

Fermio is a systemic intervention. We’ve built the bridge between the people who make batteries, the government that needs to track them, and the logistics that move them. It’s a unified loop that makes recycling as invisible and automatic as breathing.
